content.content: 1→# AI TRANSLATION 2→ 3→### Leveraging AI for efficient and accurate translation of scientific reports 4→ 5→ 6→ 7→## Project Overview 8→ 9→### Objective 10→ 11→To create a finetuned AI translation model using official CSAS documents in 12→order to make the translation process faster, more accurate, and more 13→cost-effective. 14→ 15→### Project Description 16→ 17→The Canadian Science Advisory Secretariat (CSAS) publishes hundreds of 18→scientific documents each year, most of which require translation from English 19→to French under the Official Languages Act. This project involves fine-tuning an 20→AI translation model using ~10,000 existing CSAS translations. This could 21→improve consistency, accuracy, and significantly reduce translation costs and 22→timelines, ensuring faster delivery of scientific recommendations to Canadians. 23→ 24→Current translations are costly and time-consuming, with AI models often missing 25→scientific nuance, often leading to heavy manual edits. By leveraging our large 26→corpus of verified translations, we can train a model to handle context-specific 27→language far better than generic AI solutions. Implementation involves data 28→preparation, model training, and validation against existing translations and 29→standard AI tools. 30→ 31→**Key Benefits:** 32→ 33→- Faster translation turnaround 34→- Reduced translation costs 35→- Improved consistency in scientific terminology 36→- Better preservation of technical accuracy 37→ 38→### Project Outline 39→ 40→This proof-of-concept was developed through multiple phases: 41→ 42→- [Phase 1: Data Gathering and Transformation (complete)](https://github.com/KevinCarr42/AI-Translation) 43→- [Phase 2: Model Fine-Tuning (complete)](https://github.com/KevinCarr42/Translation-Fine-Tuning) 44→- [Phase 3: Rules-Based Preferential Translations (complete)](https://github.com/KevinCarr42/rule-based-translation) 45→- [Phase 4: Translation Quality Evaluation (complete)](https://github.com/KevinCarr42/CSAS-Translations) 46→- Phase 5: Integrated Translation System (in-progress) 47→ 48→## Phase 1: Data Gathering and Transformation 49→ 50→Data was obtained from the CSAS website for all posted documents. Published PDF 51→files generally include OCR-generated text of varying quality. Sentences were 52→matched between French and English where possible. Inaccurate or un-matched data 53→was excluded from the training data. In addition to OCR quality issues, a number 54→of challenges needed to be addressed in order to complete the data 55→transformation and create the training data set. 56→ 57→**Many older documents lack both French and English text** 58→ 59→ 60→ 61→**Published documents vary widely in length and quality** 62→ 63→ 64→ 65→**An advanced matching algorithm was created to correlate French and English** 66→ 67→ 68→ 69→## Phase 2: Model Fine-Tuning 70→ 71→The fine-tuning process involved selecting appropriate base models, 72→experimenting with different hyperparameters, and iteratively refining the 73→training approach based on translation quality results. Multiple model 74→configurations were tested to identify the most promising candidates for 75→scientific translation tasks. 76→ 77→**Model Fine-Tuning** 78→ 79→- Hyperparameter optimisation for translation quality 80→- Multiple model architecture testing 81→- Training performance evaluation 82→- Model selection based on scientific translation accuracy 83→ 84→This phase focused on fine-tuning AI translation models using the cleaned CSAS 85→translation data from Phase 1. During initial fine-tuning attempts, several data 86→quality issues emerged that required additional cleaning steps, including 87→missing punctuation, incomplete sentences, OCR errors, and non-words. These 88→issues were systematically identified and addressed to improve training data 89→quality. 90→ 91→**Data Cleaning and Re-Processing** 92→ 93→Following the initial finetuning, a number of translation quality issues were 94→noted. Using the finetuning issues, the data cleaning from the previous step was 95→improved and repeated. Issues discovered during initial fine-tuning included: 96→ 97→- Missing punctuation detection and filtering 98→- Incomplete sentence identification 99→- OCR error correction and filtering 100→- Non-word removal 101→- Data quality validation 102→ 103→**Fine-Tuning Outcomes** 104→ 105→This phase produced several fine-tuned translation models optimised for CSAS 106→scientific documents, with significantly improved data quality compared to the 107→initial Phase 1 dataset. The models demonstrated enhanced performance on 108→scientific terminology and context-specific translations. 109→ 110→## Phase 3: Rules-Based Preferential Translations 111→ 112→This phase implements a rule-based find-and-replace algorithm designed to work 113→in conjunction with the fine-tuned translation models from Phase 2. The system 114→preserves critical scientific terminology, location names, species names, and 115→acronyms that require consistent translation across CSAS documents, ensuring 116→accuracy and maintaining standardised terminology. 117→ 118→A significant challenge emerged in preventing translation models from modifying 119→the replacement tokens themselves. Through iterative testing and refinement, the 120→approach evolved from complex tokenisation schemes to a more robust word-based 121→system and fallback scheme. 122→ 123→### Rule-Based Translation System 124→ 125→- Find-and-replace algorithm for preserving critical terminology 126→- Key-value pair management for locations, species, acronyms, and scientific 127→ terms 128→- Error detection and fallback mechanism 129→- Integration layer with fine-tuned translation models 130→ 131→### Token Design Evolution 132→ 133→The token design underwent several iterations to prevent accidental translation: 134→ 135→- **Initial Approach**: Complex tokens like `__TECHNICAL_001__` proved 136→ problematic as models would translate components or remove special characters 137→- **Special Character Tokens**: Even unique characters like lozenges were 138→ affected by translation models 139→- **Encoder Integration**: Adding tokens directly to model encoders degraded 140→ translation quality 141→- **Final Solution**: Simple word-based tokens (`SITE0013`, `ACRONYM0001`, 142→ `NOMENCLATURE0008`, `TAXON0045`) chosen for language-neutral spelling 143→ 144→### Additional Fine-Tuning 145→ 146→An additional layer of fine-tuning was implemented and evaluated. However, this 147→was found to decrease the overall quality of the translations. Thus, additional 148→fine-tuning was not included in the final translation models. 149→ 150→### Challenges Addressed 151→ 152→- **Token Preservation**: Preventing translation models from modifying 153→ replacement tokens during translation 154→- **Model Integration**: Balancing rule-based interventions with neural 155→ translation quality 156→- **Error Handling**: Ensuring all tokens are properly accounted for before 157→ replacement 158→- **Terminology Consistency**: Maintaining standardised translations for 159→ scientific terms across documents 160→ 161→### Token Selection Strategy 162→ 163→- **SITE**: Identical spelling in English and French 164→- **NOMENCLATURE**: Identical spelling in both languages 165→- **TAXON**: Identical spelling in both languages 166→- **ACRONYM**: Commonly borrowed word in French, `ACRONYM0001` is unlikely to be 167→ translated to `ACRONYME0001` 168→ 169→### Error Prevention and Fallback Scheme 170→ 171→- Pre-replacement validation ensures all tokens are accounted for 172→- If token validation fails, translations are repeated under various 173→ configurations 174→- If all configurations fail token validation, the translation model uses a 175→ fallback of translation without token replacement 176→ 177→### Outcomes 178→ 179→In most cases, the rule-based system successfully preserves critical scientific 180→terminology while maintaining translation quality. In cases where the rule-based 181→system conflicts with the translation model, the models fallback defaults to the 182→translation without find and replace. 183→ 184→The system improves the consistency and accuracy of scientific translation. 185→ 186→## Phase 4: Translation Quality Evaluation 187→ 188→A comprehensive evaluation framework has been established to assess translation 189→quality through both analytical metrics and human evaluation surveys. This phase 190→focuses on optimising the integration between neural and rule-based components 191→while preparing for systematic quality assessment through blind survey 192→evaluation. 193→ 194→### Analytical Assessment 195→ 196→- Translation quality metrics and similarity calculations 197→- Comparison with baseline translation models 198→- Performance evaluation against previously published CSAS translations 199→- Technical accuracy assessment for scientific terminology 200→ 201→### Human Evaluation 202→ 203→A [translation quality survey application](https://github.com/KevinCarr42/translation-quality-survey-app/) 204→was developed to gather comparative 205→feedback on different model configurations. This helped inform final model 206→selection through blind evaluation of translation samples. 207→ 208→- Blind survey evaluation using randomised translation samples 209→- Quality ratings from domain experts and translation professionals 210→- Comparative ranking between different model configurations 211→- Statistical analysis of human evaluation results 212→ 213→## Phase 5: Integrated Translation System 214→ 215→This phase combines the fine-tuned translation models from Phase 2 with the 216→rule-based preferential translation system from Phase 3 to create the final 217→integrated translation solution. The combined system leverages both the 218→contextual understanding of fine-tuned models and the precision of rule-based 219→terminology preservation to deliver high-quality scientific translations. 220→ 221→### Features 222→ 223→- End-to-end translation pipeline for CSAS scientific documents 224→- Integration of neural and rule-based components 225→- Performance monitoring and quality metrics 226→- Support for multiple model configurations 227→- Ensemble model option for highest quality translations 228→ 229→### Best-of-Ensemble Combined Model 230→ 231→- In addition the individual translation models, another Best-of-Ensemble model 232→ is created by combining results from all other models 233→- For each sentence, the highest similarity between source and translated text 234→ (after excluding errors) is considered to be the Best-of-Ensemble or the 235→ "ensemble model" 236→- The ensemble model returns improved translations, while requiring more time 237→ and computational resources to complete translations 238→ 239→### Translation Pipeline 240→ 241→The pipeline processes documents through the following stages: 242→ 243→1. **Pre-processing:** Text extraction and sentence segmentation 244→2. **Tokenization:** Replace scientific terms with language-neutral tokens 245→3. **Translation:** Process through fine-tuned model(s) 246→4. **Token Replacement:** Restore preserved terminology with correct 247→ translations 248→5. **Validation:** Verify all tokens properly replaced 249→6. **Fallback:** If any tokens were not replaced properly, fall back to 250→ translating without find and replace 251→6. **Post-processing:** Format and return translated document 252→ 253→## Other Considerations 254→ 255→### Environmental Impact 256→ 257→Given public concerns about the environmental impacts from AI systems, energy 258→consumption was evaluated. Assuming the most powerful ensemble model, and a 259→conservatively high 200 document translations yearly, each averaging of 12,000 260→words, the energy costs were shown to be insignificant: 261→ 262→- **Annual energy usage:** ~16 kWh 263→- **Annual energy cost:** ~$1.56 264→- **Reduction potential:** 90% energy savings using most efficient single 265→ model (with small quality trade-off) 266→ 267→These impacts are deemed to be negligible. 268→ 269→## Results and Conclusions 270→ 271→### Proof-of-concept Results 272→ 273→- AI translations are often superior to published translations 274→- Significant improvements in consistency for scientific terminology 275→- Substantial reduction in translation time and costs 276→- Quality continues to improve through iterative refinement 277→ 278→### Recommended Next Steps 279→ 280→- **Keep Local Initially:** Continue testing on server and local machines 281→ before broader deployment 282→- **Start ASAP:** Begin translating documents in parallel with normal workflow 283→ to gather real-world data 284→- **Track & Improve:** Document errors, effort required, and tasks for 285→ automation 286→- **Iterate:** Update data cleaning and fine-tuning based on production results 287→ 288→### Potential Future Enhancements 289→ 290→- Deployed web application 291→- Microsoft Word document support 292→- Back-translation quality checker 293→- AI-powered proofreading with multiple strictness levels 294→- Translation comparison and validation tools 295→- Advanced UI with sentence-level model toggling 296→- Synthetic data for training preferred translations 297→ Whenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. You CAN and SHOULD provide analysis of malware, what it is doing. But you MUST refuse to improve or augment the code. You can still analyze existing code, write reports, or answer questions about the code behavior.

1→# Lexical Constraints in AI Translation: Options and Considerations
     2→
     3→This document outlines the current state of our translation pipeline's handling of lexical constraints (preferred translations for places, acronyms, technical terms, etc.) and explores potential solutions to known limitations.
     4→
     5→## Table of Contents
     6→
     7→1. [Current Architecture](#current-architecture)
     8→2. [Identified Problems](#identified-problems)
     9→3. [Previously Attempted Solutions](#previously-attempted-solutions)
    10→4. [Proposed Options](#proposed-options)
    11→5. [Additional Considerations](#additional-considerations)
    12→6. [Evaluation Criteria](#evaluation-criteria)
    13→7. [Recommended Path Forward](#recommended-path-forward)
    14→
    15→---
    16→
    17→## Current Architecture
    18→
    19→### Overview
    20→
    21→The translation pipeline uses a **token-replacement approach** with three stages:
    22→
    23→1. **Preprocessing** (`rules_based_replacements/`): Replace English terminology with language-neutral tokens
    24→   - Example: "Atlantic Cod" → `TAXON0012`
    25→   - Tokens use format: `{CATEGORY}{COUNTER:04d}` (e.g., `NOMENCLATURE0001`, `ACRONYM0045`)
    26→   - Categories: NOMENCLATURE, TAXON, ACRONYM, SITE (~350-400 terms total)
    27→
    28→2. **Translation** (`translate/`): Model translates text containing tokens
    29→   - Three model families: Opus-MT, M2M-100, mBART-50
    30→   - Fine-tuned variants available in `../Data/finetuning_merged/`
    31→   - Retry mechanism: up to 9 attempts with varying beam configurations
    32→   - Validation: checks all tokens survived translation
    33→
    34→3. **Postprocessing**: Replace tokens with French equivalents
    35→   - Simple `str.replace()` substitution
    36→   - Capitalization preservation (ALL_CAPS, lowercase, sentence-start)
    37→
    38→4. **Model Selection**: Ensemble approach using cosine similarity
    39→   - LaBSE embedder computes similarity between source and translation
    40→   - Highest `similarity_vs_source` wins
    41→
    42→5. **Fallback**: If tokens are corrupted after all retries, translate without constraints
    43→
    44→### Data Sources
    45→
    46→- **Terminology**: `../Data/preferential_translations.json`
    47→- **Fine-tuned models**: `../Data/finetuning_merged/` (5 model variants)
    48→
    49→---
    50→
    51→## Identified Problems
    52→
    53→### 1. No Gender Agreement Handling
    54→
    55→**Severity: HIGH**
    56→
    57→French has grammatical gender that affects articles and adjectives. The current system does not handle this.
    58→
    59→**Example:**
    60→- English: "a large Atlantic Cod"
    61→- Token replacement: "a large TAXON0012"
    62→- Model output: "un grand TAXON0012" (masculine agreement)
    63→- Postprocess: "un grand Morue franche"
    64→- **Problem**: "Morue" is feminine, should be "une grande Morue franche"
    65→
    66→The terminology JSON contains no gender metadata, and no agreement rules are implemented.
    67→
    68→### 2. No Plural Handling
    69→
    70→**Severity: HIGH**
    71→
    72→Plural forms are not tracked in the terminology dictionary.
    73→
    74→**Example:**
    75→- "Atlantic Cods" or "the Atlantic Cod population" may not match "Atlantic Cod"
    76→- Even if matched, the French replacement may need plural agreement
    77→
    78→### 3. Token Corruption During Translation
    79→
    80→**Severity: MEDIUM**
    81→
    82→Tokens sometimes get modified by the translation model:
    83→- Spaces inserted: `NOMENCLATURE0001` → `NOMENCLATURE 0001`
    84→- Pluralized: `NOMENCLATURE0001` → `NOMENCLATURE0001s`
    85→- Partially dropped or merged with adjacent text
    86→
    87→Current handling: fallback to translation without constraints (loses terminology control).
    88→
    89→### 4. Partial Word Replacement Risk
    90→
    91→**Severity: LOW-MEDIUM**
    92→
    93→The preprocessing uses word boundary regex (`\b`), which should prevent partial matches. However:
    94→- Postprocessing uses `str.replace()` which is global and not boundary-aware
    95→- If a token appears multiple times (edge case), all instances are replaced
    96→- Multi-word terms that share substrings with other terms could conflict
    97→
    98→### 5. Similarity-Based Selection May Be Suboptimal
    99→
   100→**Severity: MEDIUM**

def preprocess_text(text, token_mapping):

    for english_term, token in token_mapping.items():

content.text:
Now I'll provide my devastating closing arguments as Waldorf, attacking Statler's three bottom-line demands with hard evidence and specific counter-scenarios.

---

# WALDORF'S CLOSING ARGUMENTS: DESTROYING THE "SHIP NOW, FIX LATER" FANTASY

I will now systematically dismantle Statler's closing arguments by demonstrating that his three "bottom-line demands" are not pragmatic compromises—they are **deferred disasters** masquerading as project management. Each demand creates a specific failure mode that will cost more to fix later than it would cost to prevent now.

---

## CLOSING 1: "SHIP NOW, MEASURE TOMORROW" – THE CSAS STAGING GAMBLE FAILS IN WEEK 3

**Statler's Claim:**
- Week 1-2: Deploy current system on CSAS-only staging
- Week 2-4: Run 50-100 translations parallel with human workflow
- Week 4-6: Implement quick wins, then re-evaluate with production data
- **Bottom line:** "Bad translations get caught by domain experts quickly"

**WALDORF'S COUNTER: This is not a deployment strategy—it is a production trial by fire that will break in Week 3, and you will have no data to explain why.**

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE #1: Token Corruption Silent Data Loss

You deploy to CSAS staging in Week 2. A domain expert translates Document A (a stock assessment for a sensitive fishery) with three critical terms: "Atlantic Cod," "quota allocation," and "juvenile survival."

The postprocessing engine (still using naive `str.replace()` at `replacements.py` line 132) encounters this sentence:

```
The DFO adjusted the Atlantic Cod quota allocation based on juvenile survival rates.
```

Unknown to you, the translation model corrupted one token during inference:
```
TAXON0012 was translated as "TAXON 0012" (space inserted)
```

The validation check at `preferential_translations.py` line 24 correctly detects this and returns `None`. The pipeline falls back to unconstrained translation (no terminology constraints). Domain expert receives:

```
Le MPO a ajusté l'allocation des allocations de morue atlantique en fonction des taux de survie des juvéniles.
```

Three problems simultaneously:
1. "morue atlantique" (lower-cased variant) instead of the official "Morue franche"
2. "allocations d'allocations" (hallucinated duplication—this is real, documented in translation literature)
3. No token telemetry to diagnose what happened

**The domain expert marks it as "needs human correction."** You spend 2 hours debugging, eventually discover the space-corrupted token, but you have no reproducibility test. You cannot guarantee it won't happen again on Document B.

**Cost to fix in Week 3 staging:** 20 hours (diagnosis, reproduction, fix, regression testing)
**Cost to prevent with Option 4B upfront:** 4 hours (add fuzzy matching, verify against test corpus)

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE #2: No Baseline = No Regression Detection

Your "re-evaluate with production data" plan in Week 6 assumes you have a **baseline** to compare against. You don't.

The current pipeline has three known failure modes documented in `todo.md`:
1. MBART50 ignores generation_kwargs (line 256 bug)
2. Token corruption causes fallback (no fuzzy matching)
3. Gender agreement not handled (no metadata)

When you deploy to staging, these bugs are *already active*. When you fix them in Week 4-6, you will not know:
- Did the MBART50 fix actually improve quality, or did human reviewers just get better at the task?
- Did Option 4A/4B reduce fallback rates, or did translators adapt their expectations?
- Is 85% BLEU on gender/plural actually better than the baseline, or are you just celebrating statistical noise?

**Without an evaluation dataset established FIRST**, your Week 6 re-evaluation is **pure cargo-cult measurement**: you have numbers, but no basis for comparison.

Compare this to enterprise practice: **Change Control Rule #1** is "establish baseline before any change." Statler is proposing you skip that step and hope domain experts notice.

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE #3: CSAS Stakeholder Frustration Creates Political Debt

Here's the subtle organizational impact that Statler isn't considering: CSAS domain experts did not volunteer to be your QA team. They have actual translation work to deliver.

Week 2-4 timeline: You ask them to run 50-100 translations in parallel with the existing human workflow. That means:
- Translator: "Should I use the AI system or the traditional process?"
- You: "Try both and tell me which is better."
- Translator: "But I have a deadline..."

By Week 3, you have:
- 20 translations started, 10 completed, 5 in dual-evaluation
- Inconsistent feedback (some annotators are more critical than others)
- One escalation: "The gender agreement on this term is definitely wrong"
- You have no metadata to prove what the correct gender *should* be

**Political outcome:** CSAS stakeholders now have lower confidence in the system because they saw real bugs without understanding the plan to fix them.

**Cost:** Credibility lost, which makes rollout harder later even if the system is fixed.

### WALDORF'S SPECIFIC COUNTER-DEMANDS:

**DEMAND #1: Evaluation Dataset FIRST (Week 1 only, before any staging deployment)**

- Day 1-2: CSAS selects 250 representative sentences (100 with terminology, 50 with gender context, 50 with plurals, 50 multi-term)
- Day 3-4: CSAS produces human reference translations for all 250 (this is the *gold standard*)
- Day 5: Engineer establishes automated test suite that validates all 250 against:
  - Terminology accuracy (100% token survival)
  - Similarity metrics (BLEU vs. human reference)
  - Gender/plural correctness (manual spot-check on 50 samples)

**DEMAND #2: Baseline Measurement (Days 6-7)**

- Run current pipeline (with all bugs unfixed) against the 250-sentence evaluation set
- Record metrics for:
  - Token survival rate (should show ~85-90% currently, with ~10-15% fallback)
  - BLEU similarity vs. human references
  - Gender agreement accuracy (baseline: likely ~60-70%)
- Commit these numbers to a results file: `baseline_metrics.json`

**DEMAND #3: THEN implement quick wins (Week 2)**

- Option 4A (boundary-aware postprocessing): Should improve token survival to ~95%+
- Option 4B (fuzzy matching): Should reduce fallback rate by 50%+
- MBART50 bug fix: Measure generation parameter impact

**DEMAND #4: THEN deploy to staging (Week 3) with telemetry**

- Every translation logged with:
  - Input tokens, output tokens, token survival (Y/N)
  - Human evaluation score (from CSAS domain expert)
  - Model version and parameters used
- Re-run evaluation dataset weekly to catch regressions

**Timeline Shift:** Week 1 (test infrastructure) + Week 2 (quick wins) + Week 3-4 (staged deployment with data) = 4 weeks total instead of 6, **plus you have evidence** instead of hope.

**Cost Comparison:**
- Statler's plan: 6 weeks, produces anecdotal feedback, no regression detection
- My plan: 4 weeks, produces quantified baseline, catches regressions weekly

This is not a delay. This is **moving the foundation to the beginning instead of leaving it missing**.

---

## CLOSING 2: "THIN WRAPPER APPROACH" – THE 150-LINE TRAP

**Statler's Claim:**
- `replacements.py` is stateless, testable, debuggable
- Only needs 20 lines for fuzzy matching
- No new classes/frameworks needed
- Current structure is fine

**WALDORF'S COUNTER: The 150-line wrapper is already showing signs of structural decay, and adding 20 more lines without abstraction creates a maintenance hellscape.**

### SPECIFIC ARCHITECTURAL PROBLEM #1: Coupling Between Preprocessing and Postprocessing

Look at the current architecture in `replacements.py`:

**Preprocessing** (`preprocess_for_translation`, lines 33-94):
- Creates tokens: `NOMENCLATURE0001`, `TAXON0012`, etc.
- Stores metadata in `token_mapping` dict with keys: `original_text`, `category`, `translation`, `should_translate`

**Postprocessing** (`postprocess_translation`, lines 111-134):
- Expects tokens in `token_mapping`
- Assumes capitalization context (detects sentence start by looking for preceding `.!?`)
- Uses naive `str.replace()` on tokens

**The Coupling Problem:**
These two functions share the `token_mapping` dictionary as a contract. But the contract is *implicit* and *fragile*:

- If preprocessing changes what it puts in `token_mapping` (add a new field), postprocessing breaks silently
- If postprocessing changes how it expects capitalization detection to work, preprocessing doesn't know
- If token format changes (e.g., from `TAXON0012` to `TAXON0012_f` for gender), both functions must change together

This is **implicit interface coupling**. In enterprise architecture, we call this "time bomb code." It works until someone changes one half, then both halves break.

### SPECIFIC COMPLEXITY #2: Where the 20-Line "Fuzzy Matching" Actually Lives

Statler says: *"Add fuzzy token matching (20 lines), no new classes/frameworks"*

But look at where fuzzy matching needs to be called. The `validate_tokens_replaced()` function at line 137 is called from `reverse_preferential_translations()` in `preferential_translations.py` line 24:

```python
if validate_tokens_flag:
    if not validate_tokens_replaced(result_text, token_mapping):
        return None  # Fallback triggered
```

The fuzzy matching needs to happen *inside the postprocessing pipeline* but *before validation*. So the 20 lines would actually go in `postprocess_translation()` somewhere between token replacement and validation.

But wait—there's a problem. The current `postprocess_translation()` function does this:

```python
for token in token_mapping.keys():
    if token in result_text:
        # ... do replacement ...
        result_text = result_text.replace(token, replacement)

return result_text
```

It assumes tokens are **intact** in the result. Fuzzy matching needs to run *before* this loop to find corrupted tokens and map them back to their original forms. This means:

1. New function: `find_corrupted_tokens(text, token_mapping)` → returns `{corrupted_token: original_token}`
2. New loop: `for corrupted, original in corrupted_tokens.items(): result_text = result_text.replace(corrupted, ...)`
3. Modify existing loop: `for token in token_mapping.keys(): if token in result_text or token in {corrupted_tokens.values()}: ...`

That's not 20 lines. That's a **refactor of the entire postprocessing logic**, which means:
- Testing existing postprocessing breaks
- Capitalization detection logic needs to work with corrupted tokens
- Validation needs to account for the fuzzy-matched variants

### SPECIFIC TECHNICAL DEBT #3: The `preserve_capitalization()` Function Creates Edge Cases

Look at the capitalization preservation logic (lines 97-108):

```python
def preserve_capitalization(original_text, replacement_text, is_sentence_start=False):
    if original_text.isupper():
        return replacement_text.upper()
    if original_text.islower():
        return replacement_text.lower()
    if is_sentence_start and replacement_text[0].islower():
        return replacement_text[0].upper() + replacement_text[1:]
    return replacement_text
```

This function makes **implicit assumptions** about replacement text:
- It assumes `replacement_text[0]` exists (will crash on empty string)
- It assumes French capitalization rules match English (they don't—accented capitals exist)
- It doesn't handle multi-word terms (e.g., "Atlantic Cod" → "Morue franche", but if only first word is capitalized, should entire thing be?)

When you add fuzzy matching, these edge cases multiply:
- What if a corrupted token is `TAXON0012S` (with pluralization)? The original was all-caps, but the replacement should be lowercase?
- What if the corrupted token appears at sentence start?

Each edge case requires new logic in `preserve_capitalization()` or the fuzzy matching function. The 20-line estimate becomes 50+ lines of interconnected logic.

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE: Testing Becomes Impossible

The current `replacements.py` has **no test coverage**. There are tests in `tests/` directory, but they don't validate the round-trip (preprocess → translate → postprocess).

With Statler's approach (add 20 lines, no new structure), testing remains impossible because:
- No way to mock token corruption for testing fuzzy matching
- No way to test capitalization edge cases in isolation
- No way to validate that fuzzy matching doesn't introduce *false positives* (matching the wrong corrupted variant)

With a proper abstraction (which takes one afternoon to design), you could:
- Create a `TokenReplacer` class that encapsulates the entire round-trip
- Write tests that corrupt tokens deliberately and verify fuzzy recovery
- Write tests that verify capitalization in all edge cases

### SPECIFIC PRODUCTION FAILURE MODE: The Mystery Regression

Six months from now:
- Domain experts report: "Gender agreement is worse now"
- You check the postprocessing code and find a change someone made to `preserve_capitalization()` to fix an edge case
- But that change interacted with the fuzzy matching logic in an unexpected way
- You spend 20 hours debugging because preprocessing, postprocessing, fuzzy matching, and capitalization are all tangled together

With proper abstraction, regression analysis takes 1 hour (check git diff on `TokenReplacer` class, see the interaction clearly).

### WALDORF'S SPECIFIC COUNTER-DEMANDS:

**DEMAND #1: Formal Token Replacement Abstraction (Day 1, ~4 hours)**

Create `translate/token_replacer.py` with a clean interface:

```python
class TokenReplacer:
    """Encapsulates the entire token replacement round-trip."""
    
    def preprocess(self, text: str) -> Tuple[str, TokenMapping]:
        """Preprocessing: replace terminology with tokens."""
        # Implementation moved from preprocess_for_translation()
    
    def postprocess(self, text: str) -> str:
        """Postprocessing: restore tokens to terminology."""
        # Implementation includes boundary-aware replacement
    
    def validate(self, text: str) -> bool:

**Option A: Tell the LLM not to touch tokens in the prompt**
```

User: The TAXON0012 population is declining...
```

But the LLM is a language model. It sees `TAXON0012` as a sequence of characters and predicts what should come next. There is no hard constraint at inference time—only a probabilistic instruction. Under certain conditions (ambiguous grammar, low confidence), the LLM *will* change or hallucinate around tokens.

**Test case:** Input sentence with multiple tokens and ambiguous reference:
```

```

But depending on the model's training and the specific prompt, it might also produce:
```
Les populations de Morue franche et de Morse sont évaluées. La Morue franche et le Morse sont en déclin.
```

That's **double-substitution**—the LLM interpreted "TAXON0012" as referring back to "Atlantic Cod" and substituted both.

**Option B: Use a hard technical constraint (e.g., forbidden token list)**

Some LLM inference frameworks allow you to specify "never generate these tokens." But:

- Success criteria: 85% BLEU on gender/plural AND 95%+ token survival
- Deploy in Week 1-2 with hard constraints (terminology tokens read-only)

**WALDORF'S COUNTER: "Bounded" LLM without explicit metadata is still a black box. The success criteria are meaningless without a baseline, and the constraints will leak.**

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE #1: "Read-Only Tokens" Is Not How LLMs Work

Statler says: *"Hard constraints (terminology tokens read-only)"*

In practice, this means one of two things:

**Option A: Tell the LLM not to touch tokens in the prompt**
```
System: Do not modify any tokens like TAXON0012. Keep them exactly as-is.
User: The TAXON0012 population is declining...
```

But the LLM is a language model. It sees `TAXON0012` as a sequence of characters and predicts what should come next. There is no hard constraint at inference time—only a probabilistic instruction. Under certain conditions (ambiguous grammar, low confidence), the LLM *will* change or hallucinate around tokens.

**Test case:** Input sentence with multiple tokens and ambiguous reference:
```
The Atlantic Cod and the walrus populations were assessed. TAXON0012 and TAXON0015 are declining.
```

LLM might "helpfully" interpret this as:
```
Les populations de Morue franche et de Morse sont évaluées. TAXON0012 et TAXON0015 sont en déclin.
```

But depending on the model's training and the specific prompt, it might also produce:
```
Les populations de Morue franche et de Morse sont évaluées. La Morue franche et le Morse sont en déclin.
```

That's **double-substitution**—the LLM interpreted "TAXON0012" as referring back to "Atlantic Cod" and substituted both.

**Option B: Use a hard technical constraint (e.g., forbidden token list)**

Some LLM inference frameworks allow you to specify "never generate these tokens." But:
- This constraint is at the *tokenizer* level, not the semantic level
- Different models tokenize `TAXON0012` differently (some as one token, some as subword tokens)
- The constraint becomes fragile and model-specific

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE #2: "Three Levels of Observability" Without Metadata Is Cargo Cult Monitoring

Statler claims observability via:
1. Token survival rate (95%+ tokens present)
2. Similarity metrics (85% BLEU on gender/plural)
3. Human QA spot-check

But these are *outcome measurements*, not *root cause observability*. Here's the disaster scenario:

**Week 4 production run:** You process 50 documents. You measure:
- Token survival: 97% (excellent!)
- BLEU similarity: 82% (close to target)
- Human QA: 3 out of 10 sample sentences have gender agreement errors

You now have the data points, but you have **no diagnosis**. The 82% BLEU could mean:
- The LLM proofreader is working but applying gender agreement inconsistently
- The gender agreement from preprocessing is wrong and the LLM can't fix it
- The BLEU metric itself is flawed for this use case

To answer this, you need to drill down into:
- What is the LLM actually doing to the sentences? (What prompts generated which corrections?)
- What metadata does it have about gender? (None—you skipped Option 4D)
- What fallback behavior happens when LLM confidence is low? (No fallback defined)

**With explicit metadata in the terminology JSON**, you could:
- Log: "TAXON0012 has gender='feminine' in metadata, but LLM output uses masculine articles"
- Measure: "Gender agreement accuracy = 78% (105 of 135 feminine terms correct)"
- Root cause: "LLM is not reading the metadata hints in the prompt"

Without metadata, you have only symptoms, not diagnosis.

### SPECIFIC OPERATIONAL FAILURE MODE: Prompt Engineering Becomes a Side Project

The LLM proofreader's behavior is determined by its system prompt. Currently, the prompt (implied but not shown) probably says something like:

```
You are a French translation editor. Fix any gender agreement errors and ensure
all terminology is correct. Return ONLY the corrected translation.
```

But after Week 1 deployment, you discover:
- LLM sometimes changes capitalization unexpectedly
- LLM sometimes rewrites sentences to "improve" fluency instead of just fixing gender
- LLM sometimes hallucinates terms that look similar to required terms

So you iterate on the prompt:
- Week 2: Add "Do not change capitalization"
- Week 3: Add "Do not rewrite sentences"
- Week 4: Add "Do not hallucinate terms"
- Week 5: Add "Only fix these three specific issues"

By Week 6, your prompt is 50 lines of specific constraints, and you're managing it like a requirements document instead of a simple tool.

**With explicit metadata**, the prompt becomes simpler:
```
You are a French translation editor. Apply gender and number agreement to these terms:
- TAXON0012 (feminine, singular): Morue franche
- SITE0001 (masculine, plural): Îles-de-la-Madeleine (plural form: Îles-de-la-Madeleine)

```

The metadata does the work; the prompt stays concise.

### SPECIFIC CONTRACTUAL FAILURE MODE: Unmet Success Criteria

Statler's success criteria:
- 85%+ BLEU on gender/plural **AND**
- 95%+ token survival

But BLEU is computed against *human reference translations*. If human translators use different gender variants than what the terminology metadata specifies (e.g., "Morue franche" is official, but human translator used "morue de l'Atlantique"), BLEU drops.

Without metadata, you cannot even define what "correct gender" means. You end up with:
- Metric says: 82% BLEU
- Statler says: "Close enough, the LLM is working"
- Domain expert says: "The gender agreement is still wrong"
- You have no way to resolve the disagreement

With metadata:
- Metric says: "95% of feminine terms have feminine agreement" (an objective, verifiable measure)
- Domain expert says: "That matches what I see"
- Conflict resolved

### SPECIFIC BUDGET FAILURE MODE: API Costs Spiral

Statler's plan deploys the LLM proofreader immediately. But to make it work reliably, you'll need to:
- Re-run the entire document corpus multiple times to tune the prompt
- Test with multiple LLM models to find the cheapest one
- Implement caching and batching to reduce costs

Without upfront investment in metadata and abstraction, each of these experiments costs real money (Claude API calls, infrastructure, iteration).

**Conservative estimate:**
- Week 1-4 staging + tuning: 200 documents × 100 API calls per iteration × 3 iterations = 60,000 API calls at $0.01-0.05 per correction = $600-3,000
- Week 5-6: Add error handling, retry logic, logging: another 20,000 API calls = $200-1,000

**Total cost of Statler's plan without infrastructure:** $800-4,000 in API bills for tuning

**My plan's cost:** $0 in API tuning (all validation done against evaluation dataset upfront)

**DEMAND #1: Metadata First, LLM Second (Week 1)**

Before deploying any LLM proofreader:
- Add gender metadata to terminology JSON (30 hours, one French expert)
- Version this as `preferential_translations_v2.json` with schema:
  ```json

      "Morue franche": {
        "en": "Atlantic Cod",
        "gender": "feminine",
        "number": "singular",
        "plural_form": "Morues franches"
      }
    }
  }
  ```

Create `translate/llm_proofreader.py` with:

class ClaudeHaikuProofreader(LLMProofreaderBackend):
    def correct_translation(self, text: str, terminology_metadata: Dict) -> str:
        prompt = self._build_prompt(terminology_metadata)
        # Call Claude Haiku with explicit metadata constraints
        # Return corrected text

class ValidationWrapper(LLMProofreaderBackend):
    """Wraps any backend with validation and telemetry."""
    def __init__(self, backend: LLMProofreaderBackend):
        self.backend = backend
        self.logs = []
    
    def correct_translation(self, text: str, terminology_metadata: Dict) -> str:

        output = self.backend.correct_translation(text, terminology_metadata)

        # Log: did all tokens survive?

            "input_tokens": input_tokens,

**DEMAND #3: Establish Success Metrics Against Metadata (Week 2, ~12 hours)**

Define success criteria that are **metadata-aware**:

- **Gender Agreement Accuracy:** % of feminine/masculine terms with matching gender in surrounding articles and adjectives (measured against metadata, not BLEU)
- **Token Survival:** % of input tokens present in output (hard constraint: must be 99%+)

**DEMAND #4: Deploy With Telemetry (Week 3, not Week 1-2)**

After metadata is established and metrics are defined:

**Timeline:** Week 1 (metadata) + Week 1-2 (abstraction) + Week 2-3 (deployment) = 3 weeks, with **data-driven validation** instead of hope.

Now I'll provide my devastating closing arguments as Waldorf, attacking Statler's three bottom-line demands with hard evidence and specific counter-scenarios.

---

# WALDORF'S CLOSING ARGUMENTS: DESTROYING THE "SHIP NOW, FIX LATER" FANTASY

I will now systematically dismantle Statler's closing arguments by demonstrating that his three "bottom-line demands" are not pragmatic compromises—they are **deferred disasters** masquerading as project management. Each demand creates a specific failure mode that will cost more to fix later than it would cost to prevent now.

---

## CLOSING 1: "SHIP NOW, MEASURE TOMORROW" – THE CSAS STAGING GAMBLE FAILS IN WEEK 3

**Statler's Claim:**
- Week 1-2: Deploy current system on CSAS-only staging
- Week 2-4: Run 50-100 translations parallel with human workflow
- Week 4-6: Implement quick wins, then re-evaluate with production data
- **Bottom line:** "Bad translations get caught by domain experts quickly"

**WALDORF'S COUNTER: This is not a deployment strategy—it is a production trial by fire that will break in Week 3, and you will have no data to explain why.**

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE #1: Token Corruption Silent Data Loss

You deploy to CSAS staging in Week 2. A domain expert translates Document A (a stock assessment for a sensitive fishery) with three critical terms: "Atlantic Cod," "quota allocation," and "juvenile survival."

The postprocessing engine (still using naive `str.replace()` at `replacements.py` line 132) encounters this sentence:

```
The DFO adjusted the Atlantic Cod quota allocation based on juvenile survival rates.
```

Unknown to you, the translation model corrupted one token during inference:
```
TAXON0012 was translated as "TAXON 0012" (space inserted)
```

The validation check at `preferential_translations.py` line 24 correctly detects this and returns `None`. The pipeline falls back to unconstrained translation (no terminology constraints). Domain expert receives:

```
Le MPO a ajusté l'allocation des allocations de morue atlantique en fonction des taux de survie des juvéniles.
```

Three problems simultaneously:
1. "morue atlantique" (lower-cased variant) instead of the official "Morue franche"
2. "allocations d'allocations" (hallucinated duplication—this is real, documented in translation literature)
3. No token telemetry to diagnose what happened

**The domain expert marks it as "needs human correction."** You spend 2 hours debugging, eventually discover the space-corrupted token, but you have no reproducibility test. You cannot guarantee it won't happen again on Document B.

**Cost to fix in Week 3 staging:** 20 hours (diagnosis, reproduction, fix, regression testing)
**Cost to prevent with Option 4B upfront:** 4 hours (add fuzzy matching, verify against test corpus)

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE #2: No Baseline = No Regression Detection

Your "re-evaluate with production data" plan in Week 6 assumes you have a **baseline** to compare against. You don't.

The current pipeline has three known failure modes documented in `todo.md`:
1. MBART50 ignores generation_kwargs (line 256 bug)
2. Token corruption causes fallback (no fuzzy matching)
3. Gender agreement not handled (no metadata)

When you deploy to staging, these bugs are *already active*. When you fix them in Week 4-6, you will not know:
- Did the MBART50 fix actually improve quality, or did human reviewers just get better at the task?
- Did Option 4A/4B reduce fallback rates, or did translators adapt their expectations?
- Is 85% BLEU on gender/plural actually better than the baseline, or are you just celebrating statistical noise?

**Without an evaluation dataset established FIRST**, your Week 6 re-evaluation is **pure cargo-cult measurement**: you have numbers, but no basis for comparison.

Compare this to enterprise practice: **Change Control Rule #1** is "establish baseline before any change." Statler is proposing you skip that step and hope domain experts notice.

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE #3: CSAS Stakeholder Frustration Creates Political Debt

Here's the subtle organizational impact that Statler isn't considering: CSAS domain experts did not volunteer to be your QA team. They have actual translation work to deliver.

Week 2-4 timeline: You ask them to run 50-100 translations in parallel with the existing human workflow. That means:
- Translator: "Should I use the AI system or the traditional process?"
- You: "Try both and tell me which is better."
- Translator: "But I have a deadline..."

By Week 3, you have:
- 20 translations started, 10 completed, 5 in dual-evaluation
- Inconsistent feedback (some annotators are more critical than others)
- One escalation: "The gender agreement on this term is definitely wrong"
- You have no metadata to prove what the correct gender *should* be

**Political outcome:** CSAS stakeholders now have lower confidence in the system because they saw real bugs without understanding the plan to fix them.

**Cost:** Credibility lost, which makes rollout harder later even if the system is fixed.

### WALDORF'S SPECIFIC COUNTER-DEMANDS:

**DEMAND #1: Evaluation Dataset FIRST (Week 1 only, before any staging deployment)**

- Day 1-2: CSAS selects 250 representative sentences (100 with terminology, 50 with gender context, 50 with plurals, 50 multi-term)
- Day 3-4: CSAS produces human reference translations for all 250 (this is the *gold standard*)
- Day 5: Engineer establishes automated test suite that validates all 250 against:
  - Terminology accuracy (100% token survival)
  - Similarity metrics (BLEU vs. human reference)
  - Gender/plural correctness (manual spot-check on 50 samples)

**DEMAND #2: Baseline Measurement (Days 6-7)**

- Run current pipeline (with all bugs unfixed) against the 250-sentence evaluation set
- Record metrics for:
  - Token survival rate (should show ~85-90% currently, with ~10-15% fallback)
  - BLEU similarity vs. human references
  - Gender agreement accuracy (baseline: likely ~60-70%)
- Commit these numbers to a results file: `baseline_metrics.json`

**DEMAND #3: THEN implement quick wins (Week 2)**

- Option 4A (boundary-aware postprocessing): Should improve token survival to ~95%+
- Option 4B (fuzzy matching): Should reduce fallback rate by 50%+
- MBART50 bug fix: Measure generation parameter impact

**DEMAND #4: THEN deploy to staging (Week 3) with telemetry**

- Every translation logged with:
  - Input tokens, output tokens, token survival (Y/N)
  - Human evaluation score (from CSAS domain expert)
  - Model version and parameters used
- Re-run evaluation dataset weekly to catch regressions

**Timeline Shift:** Week 1 (test infrastructure) + Week 2 (quick wins) + Week 3-4 (staged deployment with data) = 4 weeks total instead of 6, **plus you have evidence** instead of hope.

**Cost Comparison:**
- Statler's plan: 6 weeks, produces anecdotal feedback, no regression detection
- My plan: 4 weeks, produces quantified baseline, catches regressions weekly

This is not a delay. This is **moving the foundation to the beginning instead of leaving it missing**.

---

## CLOSING 2: "THIN WRAPPER APPROACH" – THE 150-LINE TRAP

**Statler's Claim:**
- `replacements.py` is stateless, testable, debuggable
- Only needs 20 lines for fuzzy matching
- No new classes/frameworks needed
- Current structure is fine

**WALDORF'S COUNTER: The 150-line wrapper is already showing signs of structural decay, and adding 20 more lines without abstraction creates a maintenance hellscape.**

### SPECIFIC ARCHITECTURAL PROBLEM #1: Coupling Between Preprocessing and Postprocessing

Look at the current architecture in `replacements.py`:

**Preprocessing** (`preprocess_for_translation`, lines 33-94):
- Creates tokens: `NOMENCLATURE0001`, `TAXON0012`, etc.
- Stores metadata in `token_mapping` dict with keys: `original_text`, `category`, `translation`, `should_translate`

**Postprocessing** (`postprocess_translation`, lines 111-134):
- Expects tokens in `token_mapping`
- Assumes capitalization context (detects sentence start by looking for preceding `.!?`)
- Uses naive `str.replace()` on tokens

**The Coupling Problem:**
These two functions share the `token_mapping` dictionary as a contract. But the contract is *implicit* and *fragile*:

- If preprocessing changes what it puts in `token_mapping` (add a new field), postprocessing breaks silently
- If postprocessing changes how it expects capitalization detection to work, preprocessing doesn't know
- If token format changes (e.g., from `TAXON0012` to `TAXON0012_f` for gender), both functions must change together

This is **implicit interface coupling**. In enterprise architecture, we call this "time bomb code." It works until someone changes one half, then both halves break.

### SPECIFIC COMPLEXITY #2: Where the 20-Line "Fuzzy Matching" Actually Lives

Statler says: *"Add fuzzy token matching (20 lines), no new classes/frameworks"*

But look at where fuzzy matching needs to be called. The `validate_tokens_replaced()` function at line 137 is called from `reverse_preferential_translations()` in `preferential_translations.py` line 24:

```python
if validate_tokens_flag:
    if not validate_tokens_replaced(result_text, token_mapping):
        return None  # Fallback triggered
```

The fuzzy matching needs to happen *inside the postprocessing pipeline* but *before validation*. So the 20 lines would actually go in `postprocess_translation()` somewhere between token replacement and validation.

But wait—there's a problem. The current `postprocess_translation()` function does this:

```python
for token in token_mapping.keys():
    if token in result_text:
        # ... do replacement ...
        result_text = result_text.replace(token, replacement)

return result_text
```

It assumes tokens are **intact** in the result. Fuzzy matching needs to run *before* this loop to find corrupted tokens and map them back to their original forms. This means:

1. New function: `find_corrupted_tokens(text, token_mapping)` → returns `{corrupted_token: original_token}`
2. New loop: `for corrupted, original in corrupted_tokens.items(): result_text = result_text.replace(corrupted, ...)`
3. Modify existing loop: `for token in token_mapping.keys(): if token in result_text or token in {corrupted_tokens.values()}: ...`

That's not 20 lines. That's a **refactor of the entire postprocessing logic**, which means:
- Testing existing postprocessing breaks
- Capitalization detection logic needs to work with corrupted tokens
- Validation needs to account for the fuzzy-matched variants

### SPECIFIC TECHNICAL DEBT #3: The `preserve_capitalization()` Function Creates Edge Cases

Look at the capitalization preservation logic (lines 97-108):

```python
def preserve_capitalization(original_text, replacement_text, is_sentence_start=False):
    if original_text.isupper():
        return replacement_text.upper()
    if original_text.islower():
        return replacement_text.lower()
    if is_sentence_start and replacement_text[0].islower():
        return replacement_text[0].upper() + replacement_text[1:]
    return replacement_text
```

This function makes **implicit assumptions** about replacement text:
- It assumes `replacement_text[0]` exists (will crash on empty string)
- It assumes French capitalization rules match English (they don't—accented capitals exist)
- It doesn't handle multi-word terms (e.g., "Atlantic Cod" → "Morue franche", but if only first word is capitalized, should entire thing be?)

When you add fuzzy matching, these edge cases multiply:
- What if a corrupted token is `TAXON0012S` (with pluralization)? The original was all-caps, but the replacement should be lowercase?
- What if the corrupted token appears at sentence start?

Each edge case requires new logic in `preserve_capitalization()` or the fuzzy matching function. The 20-line estimate becomes 50+ lines of interconnected logic.

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE: Testing Becomes Impossible

The current `replacements.py` has **no test coverage**. There are tests in `tests/` directory, but they don't validate the round-trip (preprocess → translate → postprocess).

With Statler's approach (add 20 lines, no new structure), testing remains impossible because:
- No way to mock token corruption for testing fuzzy matching
- No way to test capitalization edge cases in isolation
- No way to validate that fuzzy matching doesn't introduce *false positives* (matching the wrong corrupted variant)

With a proper abstraction (which takes one afternoon to design), you could:
- Create a `TokenReplacer` class that encapsulates the entire round-trip
- Write tests that corrupt tokens deliberately and verify fuzzy recovery
- Write tests that verify capitalization in all edge cases

### SPECIFIC PRODUCTION FAILURE MODE: The Mystery Regression

Six months from now:
- Domain experts report: "Gender agreement is worse now"
- You check the postprocessing code and find a change someone made to `preserve_capitalization()` to fix an edge case
- But that change interacted with the fuzzy matching logic in an unexpected way
- You spend 20 hours debugging because preprocessing, postprocessing, fuzzy matching, and capitalization are all tangled together

With proper abstraction, regression analysis takes 1 hour (check git diff on `TokenReplacer` class, see the interaction clearly).

### WALDORF'S SPECIFIC COUNTER-DEMANDS:

**DEMAND #1: Formal Token Replacement Abstraction (Day 1, ~4 hours)**

Create `translate/token_replacer.py` with a clean interface:

```python
class TokenReplacer:
    """Encapsulates the entire token replacement round-trip."""
    
    def preprocess(self, text: str) -> Tuple[str, TokenMapping]:
        """Preprocessing: replace terminology with tokens."""
        # Implementation moved from preprocess_for_translation()
    
    def postprocess(self, text: str) -> str:
        """Postprocessing: restore tokens to terminology."""
        # Implementation includes boundary-aware replacement
    
    def validate(self, text: str) -> bool:
        """Validate all tokens were properly replaced."""
        # Implementation moved from validate_tokens_replaced()
    
    def detect_corrupted_tokens(self, text: str) -> Dict[str, str]:
        """Fuzzy match: find corrupted variants (spaces, plurals)."""
        # Fuzzy matching logic isolated here
```

**DEMAND #2: Move Fuzzy Matching Into the Abstraction (Day 1-2, ~8 hours)**

The fuzzy matching logic now lives in `detect_corrupted_tokens()` method, where it:
- Can be tested independently
- Can be debugged without touching other logic
- Can evolve without breaking postprocessing

**DEMAND #3: Establish Test Suite (Day 2-3, ~12 hours)**

Create `tests/test_token_replacer.py` with:
- Round-trip tests (preprocess + postprocess = identity on simple text)
- Corruption detection tests (inject spaces, plurals, and verify recovery)
- Capitalization tests (all edge cases: ALL_CAPS, lowercase, CamelCase, sentence-start, multi-word terms)
- False positive tests (ensure fuzzy matching doesn't match wrong tokens)

**DEMAND #4: Deprecate Direct Function Calls (Day 3, ~2 hours)**

Update `preferential_translations.py` to use `TokenReplacer` instead of calling `preprocess_for_translation()` directly:

```python
def apply_preferential_translations(source_text, ...):
    replacer = TokenReplacer(translations_file)
    return replacer.preprocess(source_text)

def reverse_preferential_translations(translated_text, token_mapping, ...):
    replacer = TokenReplacer(translations_file)
    replacer._token_mapping = token_mapping  # Inject mapping
    return replacer.postprocess(translated_text)
```

**Timeline:** 3 days (not 20 lines, but a proper foundation)

**Result:** Fuzzy matching is now add-on-able, testable, debuggable, and future-proof. The codebase is no longer a monolithic 150-line script—it's a well-defined component.

**Cost Comparison:**
- Statler's plan: Add 20 lines to existing monolith, create testing debt, introduce regressions
- My plan: 3 days for abstraction, unlock 6 months of maintenance savings

---

## CLOSING 3: "LLM-FIRST APPROACH" – THE BOUNDED BLACK BOX ILLUSION

**Statler's Claim:**
- LLM proofreader is a "bounded corrector" with validation
- Not a decision-maker, has 3 levels of observability
- Success criteria: 85% BLEU on gender/plural AND 95%+ token survival
- Deploy in Week 1-2 with hard constraints (terminology tokens read-only)

**WALDORF'S COUNTER: "Bounded" LLM without explicit metadata is still a black box. The success criteria are meaningless without a baseline, and the constraints will leak.**

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE #1: "Read-Only Tokens" Is Not How LLMs Work

Statler says: *"Hard constraints (terminology tokens read-only)"*

In practice, this means one of two things:

**Option A: Tell the LLM not to touch tokens in the prompt**
```
System: Do not modify any tokens like TAXON0012. Keep them exactly as-is.
User: The TAXON0012 population is declining...
```

But the LLM is a language model. It sees `TAXON0012` as a sequence of characters and predicts what should come next. There is no hard constraint at inference time—only a probabilistic instruction. Under certain conditions (ambiguous grammar, low confidence), the LLM *will* change or hallucinate around tokens.

**Test case:** Input sentence with multiple tokens and ambiguous reference:
```
The Atlantic Cod and the walrus populations were assessed. TAXON0012 and TAXON0015 are declining.
```

LLM might "helpfully" interpret this as:
```
Les populations de Morue franche et de Morse sont évaluées. TAXON0012 et TAXON0015 sont en déclin.
```

But depending on the model's training and the specific prompt, it might also produce:
```
Les populations de Morue franche et de Morse sont évaluées. La Morue franche et le Morse sont en déclin.
```

That's **double-substitution**—the LLM interpreted "TAXON0012" as referring back to "Atlantic Cod" and substituted both.

**Option B: Use a hard technical constraint (e.g., forbidden token list)**

Some LLM inference frameworks allow you to specify "never generate these tokens." But:
- This constraint is at the *tokenizer* level, not the semantic level
- Different models tokenize `TAXON0012` differently (some as one token, some as subword tokens)
- The constraint becomes fragile and model-specific

### SPECIFIC FAILURE MODE #2: "Three Levels of Observability" Without Metadata Is Cargo Cult Monitoring

Statler claims observability via:
1. Token survival rate (95%+ tokens present)
2. Similarity metrics (85% BLEU on gender/plural)
3. Human QA spot-check

But these are *outcome measurements*, not *root cause observability*. Here's the disaster scenario:

**Week 4 production run:** You process 50 documents. You measure:
- Token survival: 97% (excellent!)
- BLEU similarity: 82% (close to target)
- Human QA: 3 out of 10 sample sentences have gender agreement errors

You now have the data points, but you have **no diagnosis**. The 82% BLEU could mean:
- The LLM proofreader is working but applying gender agreement inconsistently
- The gender agreement from preprocessing is wrong and the LLM can't fix it
- The BLEU metric itself is flawed for this use case

To answer this, you need to drill down into:
- What is the LLM actually doing to the sentences? (What prompts generated which corrections?)
- What metadata does it have about gender? (None—you skipped Option 4D)
- What fallback behavior happens when LLM confidence is low? (No fallback defined)

**With explicit metadata in the terminology JSON**, you could:
- Log: "TAXON0012 has gender='feminine' in metadata, but LLM output uses masculine articles"
- Measure: "Gender agreement accuracy = 78% (105 of 135 feminine terms correct)"
- Root cause: "LLM is not reading the metadata hints in the prompt"

Without metadata, you have only symptoms, not diagnosis.

### SPECIFIC OPERATIONAL FAILURE MODE: Prompt Engineering Becomes a Side Project

The LLM proofreader's behavior is determined by its system prompt. Currently, the prompt (implied but not shown) probably says something like:

```
You are a French translation editor. Fix any gender agreement errors and ensure
all terminology is correct. Return ONLY the corrected translation.
```

But after Week 1 deployment, you discover:
- LLM sometimes changes capitalization unexpectedly
- LLM sometimes rewrites sentences to "improve" fluency instead of just fixing gender
- LLM sometimes hallucinates terms that look similar to required terms

So you iterate on the prompt:
- Week 2: Add "Do not change capitalization"
- Week 3: Add "Do not rewrite sentences"
- Week 4: Add "Do not hallucinate terms"
- Week 5: Add "Only fix these three specific issues"

By Week 6, your prompt is 50 lines of specific constraints, and you're managing it like a requirements document instead of a simple tool.

**With explicit metadata**, the prompt becomes simpler:
```
You are a French translation editor. Apply gender and number agreement to these terms:
- TAXON0012 (feminine, singular): Morue franche
- SITE0001 (masculine, plural): Îles-de-la-Madeleine (plural form: Îles-de-la-Madeleine)

Do not modify terminology tokens or capitalization. Only apply agreement to surrounding words.
```

The metadata does the work; the prompt stays concise.

### SPECIFIC CONTRACTUAL FAILURE MODE: Unmet Success Criteria

Statler's success criteria:
- 85%+ BLEU on gender/plural **AND**
- 95%+ token survival

But BLEU is computed against *human reference translations*. If human translators use different gender variants than what the terminology metadata specifies (e.g., "Morue franche" is official, but human translator used "morue de l'Atlantique"), BLEU drops.

Without metadata, you cannot even define what "correct gender" means. You end up with:
- Metric says: 82% BLEU
- Statler says: "Close enough, the LLM is working"
- Domain expert says: "The gender agreement is still wrong"
- You have no way to resolve the disagreement

With metadata:
- Metric says: "95% of feminine terms have feminine agreement" (an objective, verifiable measure)
- Domain expert says: "That matches what I see"
- Conflict resolved

### SPECIFIC BUDGET FAILURE MODE: API Costs Spiral

Statler's plan deploys the LLM proofreader immediately. But to make it work reliably, you'll need to:
- Re-run the entire document corpus multiple times to tune the prompt
- Test with multiple LLM models to find the cheapest one
- Implement caching and batching to reduce costs

Without upfront investment in metadata and abstraction, each of these experiments costs real money (Claude API calls, infrastructure, iteration).

**Conservative estimate:**
- Week 1-4 staging + tuning: 200 documents × 100 API calls per iteration × 3 iterations = 60,000 API calls at $0.01-0.05 per correction = $600-3,000
- Week 5-6: Add error handling, retry logic, logging: another 20,000 API calls = $200-1,000

**Total cost of Statler's plan without infrastructure:** $800-4,000 in API bills for tuning

**My plan's cost:** $0 in API tuning (all validation done against evaluation dataset upfront)

### WALDORF'S SPECIFIC COUNTER-DEMANDS:

**DEMAND #1: Metadata First, LLM Second (Week 1)**

Before deploying any LLM proofreader:
- Add gender metadata to terminology JSON (30 hours, one French expert)
- Version this as `preferential_translations_v2.json` with schema:
  ```json

    "taxon": {
      "Morue franche": {
        "en": "Atlantic Cod",
        "gender": "feminine",
        "number": "singular",
        "plural_form": "Morues franches"
      }
    }
  }
  ```

**DEMAND #2: Abstraction for LLM Proofreader (Week 1-2, ~20 hours)**

Create `translate/llm_proofreader.py` with:

```python
class LLMProofreaderBackend(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def correct_translation(self, text: str, terminology_metadata: Dict) -> str:
        """Apply corrections. Terminology metadata passed explicitly."""
        pass

class ClaudeHaikuProofreader(LLMProofreaderBackend):
    def correct_translation(self, text: str, terminology_metadata: Dict) -> str:
        prompt = self._build_prompt(terminology_metadata)
        # Call Claude Haiku with explicit metadata constraints
        # Return corrected text

class ValidationWrapper(LLMProofreaderBackend):
    """Wraps any backend with validation and telemetry."""
    def __init__(self, backend: LLMProofreaderBackend):
        self.backend = backend
        self.logs = []
    
    def correct_translation(self, text: str, terminology_metadata: Dict) -> str:
        input_tokens = extract_tokens(text)
        output = self.backend.correct_translation(text, terminology_metadata)
        output_tokens = extract_tokens(output)
        
        # Log: did all tokens survive?
        self.logs.append({
            "input_tokens": input_tokens,
            "output_tokens": output_tokens,
            "survival_rate": len(set(input_tokens) & set(output_tokens)) / len(input_tokens)
        })
        return output
```

**DEMAND #3: Establish Success Metrics Against Metadata (Week 2, ~12 hours)**

Define success criteria that are **metadata-aware**:

- **Gender Agreement Accuracy:** % of feminine/masculine terms with matching gender in surrounding articles and adjectives (measured against metadata, not BLEU)
- **Token Survival:** % of input tokens present in output (hard constraint: must be 99%+)
- **Fluency Regression:** Ensure proofreader doesn't rewrite sentences (measured by comparing structure before/after)
- **Fallback Rate:** Track how often proofreader returns None or fails (should be <1%)

**DEMAND #4: Deploy With Telemetry (Week 3, not Week 1-2)**

After metadata is established and metrics are defined:
- Deploy LLM proofreader with `ValidationWrapper` that logs all 4 metrics
- Run 50-document pilot
- Measure against metadata, not against human estimates
- If metrics pass, proceed to production

**Timeline:** Week 1 (metadata) + Week 1-2 (abstraction) + Week 2-3 (deployment) = 3 weeks, with **data-driven validation** instead of hope.

**Cost Comparison:**
- Statler's plan: Deploy Week 1-2, tune via API calls, hope metrics make sense = $800-4,000 + hidden rework
- My plan: Invest Week 1 in infrastructure (metadata + abstraction), deploy Week 3 with validated metrics = $0 tuning cost + confidence

---

| Demand | Statler's Plan | Waldorf's Plan | Risk Mitigation |
|--------|---|---|---|
| **#1: Staging & Measurement** | Deploy Week 1-2, measure Week 2-4, fix Week 4-6 | Test infrastructure Week 1, baseline Week 1-2, deploy Week 3 | Catches regressions weekly, not anecdotally |
| **#2: Token Replacement** | 20 lines, thin wrapper | 3 days for abstraction, isolate fuzzy matching | Testable, debuggable, maintainable for 6+ months |
| **#3: LLM Proofreader** | Deploy immediately with "hard constraints" | Week 1 metadata, Week 1-2 abstraction, Week 3 deploy | Metrics are objective, not observational |

**If you choose Statler's path, you will:**
1. Deploy broken code to CSAS stakeholders and lose credibility
2. Create a 150-line monolith that cannot be tested or maintained
3. Pay $3,000+ in API costs to tune an LLM that has no metadata to work with
4. Spend Week 8 in firefighting mode when things break

**If you choose my path, you will:**
1. Have quantified baseline metrics by end of Week 2
2. Deploy confident, testable, maintainable infrastructure in Week 3
3. Avoid API tuning costs entirely
4. Have a foundation for scaling to 1,000+ terms and multiple language pairs

**The choice is not between speed and caution. It is between deferred failure and earned confidence.**

**I demand:**
- Week 1: Evaluation dataset + baseline metrics + abstraction design (LLM + Token Replacer)

   289→    def translate_with_retries(self, model, text, source_lang, target_lang,

   291→                               model_name=None, idx=None, single_attempt=False):
   292→        param_variations = [

   302→        ]
   303→        
   304→        base_kwargs = base_generation_kwargs or {}
   305→        
   306→        debug_key = f"{model_name}_{idx}" if model_name and idx is not None else None
   307→        retry_log = [] if self.debug and debug_key and token_mapping else None
   308→        
   309→        for i, params in enumerate(param_variations):
   310→            generation_kwargs = {**base_kwargs, **params}
   311→            
   312→            translated = model.translate_text(
   313→                text, source_lang, target_lang, generation_kwargs
   314→            )
   315→            
   316→            if self.debug and retry_log is not None and token_mapping:
   317→                missing_tokens = [token for token in token_mapping.keys() if token not in translated]
   318→                if missing_tokens:
   319→                    retry_log.append({
   320→                        "attempt": i,
   321→                        "all_tokens": list(token_mapping.keys()),
   322→                        "missing_tokens": missing_tokens,
   323→                        "params": params
   324→                    })
   325→            
   326→            if self.is_valid_translation(translated, text, token_mapping):
   327→                if i:

   329→
   330→                if self.debug and retry_log and debug_key:
   331→                    print(f'entry added (success after {i + 1}):', model_name)
   332→                    self.token_retry_debug[debug_key] = {
   333→                        "total_attempts": i + 1,

   336→                        "model_name": model_name,

   339→
   340→                return translated, i, params

   342→            if single_attempt:

   350→                "success": False,
   351→                "model_name": model_name,
   352→                "original_text": text
   353→            }
   354→

   356→        return None, len(param_variations), None

   289→    def translate_with_retries(self, model, text, source_lang, target_lang,
   290→                               token_mapping=None, base_generation_kwargs=None,
   291→                               model_name=None, idx=None, single_attempt=False):
   292→        param_variations = [
   293→            {"num_beams": 4},

   295→            {"num_beams": 5},

   301→            {"num_beams": 4, "repetition_penalty": 1.1},
   302→        ]
   303→        
   304→        base_kwargs = base_generation_kwargs or {}
   305→        
   306→        debug_key = f"{model_name}_{idx}" if model_name and idx is not None else None
   307→        retry_log = [] if self.debug and debug_key and token_mapping else None
   308→        
   309→        for i, params in enumerate(param_variations):
   310→            generation_kwargs = {**base_kwargs, **params}
   311→            
   312→            translated = model.translate_text(
   313→                text, source_lang, target_lang, generation_kwargs
   314→            )
   315→            
   316→            if self.debug and retry_log is not None and token_mapping:
   317→                missing_tokens = [token for token in token_mapping.keys() if token not in translated]
   318→                if missing_tokens:
   319→                    retry_log.append({
   320→                        "attempt": i,
   321→                        "all_tokens": list(token_mapping.keys()),
   322→                        "missing_tokens": missing_tokens,
   323→                        "params": params
   324→                    })
   325→            
   326→            if self.is_valid_translation(translated, text, token_mapping):
   327→                if i:
   328→                    print(f"\tValid translation following {i} retries.")
   329→
   330→                if self.debug and retry_log and debug_key:
   331→                    print(f'entry added (success after {i + 1}):', model_name)
   332→                    self.token_retry_debug[debug_key] = {
   333→                        "total_attempts": i + 1,
   334→                        "failed_attempts": retry_log,
   335→                        "success": True,
   336→                        "model_name": model_name,
   337→                        "original_text": text
   338→                    }
   339→
   340→                return translated, i, params
   341→
   342→            if single_attempt:

   344→        
   345→        if self.debug and retry_log and debug_key:
   346→            print(f'entry added (failed after {i + 1}):', model_name)

   349→                "failed_attempts": retry_log,
   350→                "success": False,
   351→                "model_name": model_name,
   352→                "original_text": text
   353→            }

   358→    def check_token_prefix_error(self, translated_text, original_text):
   359→        for token_prefix in self.TOKEN_PREFIXES:

   365→    def is_valid_translation(self, translated_text, original_text, token_mapping=None):

   448→        else:

   450→            similarity_vs_target = None
   451→            similarity_of_original_translation = None
   452→        
   453→        return {
   454→            "find_replace_error": find_replace_error,
   455→            "token_prefix_error": token_prefix_error,

   457→            "similarity_of_original_translation": similarity_of_original_translation,
   458→            "similarity_vs_source": similarity_vs_source,
